newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: More South African consumers defaulting on debts.
newsitem.headline: More South African consumers defaulting on debts.

text.p: High South African interest rates have led to a growing number of consumers being unable to repay their debts.

And with little prospect of a rate cut until possibly the fourth quarter of this year, analysts say more and more consumers, already spending two-thirds of their personal disposable income on debt, will face bad debt judgements.

Latest Central Statistical Service (CSS) data shows the number of civil summonses for debt rose 13.5 percent year-on-year in January, while the number of judgements increased 11.5 percent -- the most dramatic increase in 10 years, according to the Information Trust Corporation (ITC).
ITC business analyst Jaco van Jaarsveldt believes the situation will get worse.

"The longer interest rates remain at current high levels, the more consumers will find themselves in a position where they can not afford the high debt repayments, and therefore one would see an increase in bad debt statistics," he said.
Having earlier discounted up to three one percentage point rate cuts this year, economists are now expecting the Reserve Bank will manage just one rate by year-end.

Their expectations have been curtailed by the private sector's insatiable appetite for credit -- a factor which central bank Governor Chris Stals has insisted must be brought under control before he considers an interest rate cut.
Private sector demand for credit ballooned to almost 380 billion rand in February -- the latest statistics available -- up 17.34 percent from a year ago and 1.8 percent month-on-month.

Economists believe one of the major reasons for the continued growth in credit extension is that local corporates have switched trade credits back onshore as the Reserve Bank's withdrawal from the forward market pushes the cost of forward cover higher.
Van Jaarsveldt said another important reason for the recent increase in credit extension growth stemmed from corporates running into liquidity problems as consumer spending slowed.
"The feeling is that the companies have stock that they can't sell. They are having to draw on their overdrafts at the banks to be able to stay liquid," he said.
"And if economic activity does not increase, it could result in an increase in liquidations," he added.
In February, CSS data shows that 262 businesses were liquidated, up from 223 a year ago, but down from 275 in January. In 1996, an average of 272 businesses were liquidated every month.
Nedcor economist Kevin Lings said the increase in bad debt judgements and liquidations corresponded with the slowdown in the business cycle.
"The expectation is that the level of bad debts will increase during the course of this year...Typically these things start to pick up when there is a slowdown in the business cycle," Lings said.

He added that while banks and retailers were usually conservative in their bad debt provisions, the increase in consumer debt defaults could also lead to an increase in banks' provisions over the next twelve months.

"In essence, people have become highly indebted, they have taken a lot of credit, interest rates are high and therefore the ability to continue to afford it at those levels becomes more difficult," Lings said.
"Under those circumstances bad debt starts to rise."
